Cardi

CurvesGeometryConstructions
Game: A small circle rolls round a fixed circle, and a dot on its rim draws a heart-shaped curve.
How to play: Drag the dot M or the touching point T. Press Play to roll the circle, pick a construction, or press Reset to start again.
Look for the math

A circle rolling round another circle of the same size makes a point on its rim draw a cardioid. The picture here shows four different ways to build that one curve.

Two circles, one heart

Let the fixed circle have centre O and radius r, and the rolling circle centre P and the same radius r. The centres are always 2r apart, so when P has turned through an angle t we have P = O + 2r(cos t, sin t). Because the circles do not slip, the mark M turns twice as fast about P: its offset from P is −r(cos 2t, sin 2t), and

M = O + 2r(cos t, sin t) − r(cos 2t, sin 2t).

At t = 0 the mark sits at the cusp A on the fixed circle. The logic test follows the applet's step-by-step rotation hundreds of times and finds exactly this formula. This is a special epicycloid: the equal radii are what give the single sharp point.

A mirror in the tangent

T is the point where the two circles touch, halfway between O and P. The arcs from T to A and from T to M are the same length, so the two chords TA and TM are equal too. That makes the tangent at T the mirror line of A and M: reflect A in every tangent of the fixed circle and you get every point of the cardioid. The midpoint of AM is the foot of the perpendicular from A to that tangent, which is why the cardioid is also the pedal curve of the circle.

Chords through the cusp

Extend the line from A through M until it meets the curve again at N. In this picture N is the mark half a turn later, and the chord MN is always 4r: the two pieces have lengths 2r(1 − cos t) and 2r(1 + cos t). Their midpoint goes round the fixed circle. The test checks both facts at more than six hundred angles, including the cusp itself.

A hinged parallelogram

Draw OQ equal and parallel to PM. Then OPMQ is a parallelogram with OP = 2·OQ: Q simply runs twice as fast as P around O, and M = P + OQ lands on the cardioid. Doubling the rod MQ through Q gives the other end N of the chord above. The old applet also contains a formula-based drawing mode that Cardi never switches on; the test uses it to check the mark's positions, and notes that its moving centre is a quarter turn out — a leftover from another cycloid applet.

Try dragging M slowly towards the cusp: the mark nearly stops there, then speeds up as it moves away.

Puzzle by Alexander Bogomolny (cut-the-knot.org)
